sections.title: Markets
sections.body:
The key new development since yesterday is the Hormuz deal optimism dimming — Iran denied direct negotiations with the US, which is moving futures this morning. That's a genuine update. Let me now compile this.

**The new since yesterday:**
- Iran denied engaging in direct negotiations with the US, dampening hopes of a Hormuz deal and pushing S&P futures lower Monday morning
- Asia bounced overnight (Nikkei +0.54%), tracking Friday's jobs-driven US rally
- European markets are a fresh story — the Stoxx 600 context and fund manager positioning shift
- Friday's root cause: soft July jobs report reduced Fed rate-hike urgency, which drove Friday's S&P record
- Japan household spending miss adds a domestic Japan headwind

---

**The Hormuz situation is the NEW element** — yesterday I told Sam the draft plan was the key watch. Now there's an actual update: Iran has publicly denied talks are happening, which is material.

The Friday jobs print driving Friday's gains is background context Sam already had (I mentioned the S&P close and VIX). But the *cause* (soft jobs → Fed hold → rally) was not fully explained yesterday — I focused on oil/Hormuz. So I can briefly note it as causal context for Monday's opening position.

Here's my section:

---

The dominant overnight development is a **deflation of Hormuz optimism**. 
Investor optimism that the US and Iran might be close to an agreement on free transit of the Hormuz strait dimmed over the weekend after Iran denied engaging in any direct negotiations with the US.
 That denial is the reason 
S&P 500 futures edged lower early Monday amid growing doubts that a deal is imminent.
 Oil holding near $78/barrel reflects the same unease.

The Friday rally that sets today's starting point had a distinct cause: 
US equity markets ended Friday at a record high after the July jobs report showed an unexpected decline in payrolls — investors focused on the softer wage and hiring trends, which may reduce inflationary pressure and give the Fed less urgency to hike rates.
 
Bond yields declined, with the 10-year Treasury near 4.64%.
 That's the rate-expectations logic underpinning the current equity level.

In Asia this morning, 
the Nikkei 225 added over 0.54% while the Kospi gained 0.53%
 — a partial catch-up to Friday's US move. Friday's Nikkei had been weighed by two separate headwinds: 
a rebound in oil prices on Hormuz tensions, and domestic data showing Japan's household spending fell 3.3% in June, defying expectations for a 1% increase.


European markets are in a structurally stronger position than they've been all year. 
The Stoxx 600 has rallied 11% year-to-date, with the DAX, CAC 40, and Italian FTSE MIB hitting all-time peaks.
 The institutional shift is notable: 
a net 2% of fund managers are now overweight European equities, compared with 15% who were underweight in June.
 The FTSE 100 is participating but structurally lags continental peers because 
London's energy-heavy composition means its fortunes on any given day are disproportionately shaped by commodity prices
 rather than the tech and growth earnings driving the DAX.

**In the portfolio:** ASML +2.15% continues to benefit from the tech-friendly rate backdrop — 
ASML was among the top performers in the Euro Stoxx 50 last week.
 AMD -1.21% is a drag; the two chip names are diverging because ASML is equipment (picks-and-shovels, less exposed to end-demand risk) while AMD is more sensitive to near-term AI spending sentiment. IJPN's +0.78% likely reflects this morning's Nikkei bounce. BAE +0.91% and QinetiQ +1.19% continue firm.

**Watch:** Iran's public denial of US talks is the live variable. If it hardens, oil moves up, yields follow, and the whole rate-cut narrative gets repriced against equities currently sitting at record multiples.

sections.title: Data & BI
sections.body:
Nothing from the BigQuery or semantic layer searches is genuinely new since yesterday's section — the BigQuery items are from April/May, the Looker self-service Explores item is from June, and the semantic layer stories are older summaries or the Snowflake Autopilot item already covered yesterday. The July Power BI feature summary, however, contains two items not covered yesterday: **TMDL View on the web** and the change to **downloading a .pbix from a semantic model**. These are substantive and fresh enough to report.

---

**Data & BI** · 10 August 2026

Two further items from the July Power BI feature summary worth flagging — neither was in yesterday's briefing.

**TMDL View lands in the Power BI Service**


The July update ships TMDL View on the web
 — meaning you can now inspect and edit Tabular Model Definition Language directly in the browser, not just in Desktop. This matters for teams who do model review or light edits on machines without Desktop installed, and makes TMDL a more credible standard for source-controlled semantic model development.

**Downloading a .pbix from a semantic model now behaves differently**


When you download a .pbix from a semantic model, you now get an empty report with the dataset only; to get the report with the dataset, you go to the report itself in the Service. The change is intended to fix inconsistent results that came from downloading via the semantic model route.


If your team or end users have documented a "download and share" workflow that starts from the semantic model, those steps now produce a different artefact. Worth checking any runbooks or support docs.

sections.title: Career & Data Leadership
sections.body:
**Hiring conditions**


UK job vacancies have continued their multi-year decline, sitting around 717,000 in the July–September window
 — yet data roles remain largely insulated. 
LinkedIn's Jobs on the Rise 2026 report makes clear that AI and data roles are leading the market, not merely participating in it, as organisations accelerate adoption and push for greater value from data assets.
 
Roles such as AI Engineer and Head of AI sit at the top of the fastest-growing jobs list
 — Head of Data sits in the same hiring cluster and benefits from the same scarcity premium.

**Geography & the Milton Keynes angle**


Remote working has compressed but not eliminated the London premium — London roles still pay roughly 20–30% more than equivalents in Manchester, Leeds, and Birmingham, though purchasing power is broadly comparable once cost of living is factored in.
 For a Milton Keynes–based senior hire, that London differential is narrowing further; roles that allow hybrid working from the Midlands/South Midlands corridor are increasingly competitive on total reward.

**Leadership lens — foundations before outputs**

Fresh practical signal from practitioners: 
analytics leaders are being advised to shift effort away from building more outputs and toward fixing the foundations those outputs depend on — starting by consolidating where critical KPIs are defined differently across teams into shared, governed semantic layers.
 The sharper framing from [The Executive Outlook](https://theexecutiveoutlook.com/blogs/effective-data-leadership-tips-lead-drive-impact-2026): 
the impact ceiling of any data programme is set by the analytical capability of the business leaders consuming its outputs — a sophisticated analytics capability serving a low–data-literacy leadership team produces underutilised insight and frustrated data teams.
 That's a concrete interview narrative: your job isn't building the platform, it's raising the floor of the business around it.


Candidate mobility is increasing — 66% of data specialists are open to new opportunities this year
, which cuts both ways: competition for roles is real, but so is the window to move.

sections.title: UK Insurance
sections.body:
**UK Insurance**

**Motor: losses deepening, pricing turn now under way**


EY's latest analysis (published late July) forecasts the UK motor market will remain loss-making through 2026 and 2027. After a profitable 2024 (NCR 98%), the market slipped back into the red in 2025 at an estimated NCR of 102%, with a worse 108% now forecast for this year.
 
The weaker outlook is driven primarily by premium rate reductions since late 2024 feeding through to earned premium, alongside persistent claims inflation.


Pricing is now turning. 
After premiums fell almost 12% during 2025, EY expects motor premiums to rise 4% in 2026 and a further 12% in 2027.
 
Defaqto also expects increases in the coming months, though any rises are more likely to be gradual and targeted rather than the sharp spikes of the last hard-market cycle.


Watch the Consumer Duty angle here: 
as the softening cycle ends, divergence in pricing decisions between carriers is likely to intensify policyholder price sensitivity at renewal and generate Consumer Duty compliance scrutiny where some insurers move sharply whilst others hold.


**FCA: rule simplification now live**


FCA insurance rule changes came into force in June and July 2026, with most taking effect on 26 June and remaining provisions on 27 July (Handbook Notice No. 142).
 
Building on its December 2025 Policy Statement, the FCA is leaning more heavily on Consumer Duty rather than introducing new product-specific or product governance requirements.
 
Further consultations are planned on simplifying GAP insurance rules, general insurance pricing data, and information disclosure requirements.
 Operationally, the compliance burden shifts from rule-checking to evidencing good outcomes — a different discipline for most personal lines teams.

**Distribution: John Lewis home panel expands**


John Lewis Money has added a personal lines specialist insurer to its home panel
 — worth tracking alongside the IKEA/Urban Jungle move flagged yesterday; both signal that retail brands are actively building out home insurance distribution rather than treating it as a static panel arrangement.

**MGA sector: AI governance now the dominant theme**


At MGAA 2026 last week, the conversation shifted firmly away from AI experimentation and towards responsible deployment, with governance, accountability and decision intelligence becoming central themes.
 
Separately, the FCA's focus on proving good customer outcomes is already shifting insurers' AI priorities from adoption to governance
 — regulatory and market pressure now pointing in the same direction.

sections.title: Milton Keynes
sections.body:
I'll search across several angles to find what's new today for Milton Keynes.
Nothing from the searches moves the needle significantly on MK Tech Week or the other stories already covered yesterday. The genuinely new items are: the Stantonbury School Ofsted special measures ruling, the MK City of Culture 2029 bid, the FlixBus coach connectivity story, and the Stagecoach driver community story. Let me use these.

**Events — diary these**

- **📅 8 Oct** — 
Powered Up Business Networking returns to The Dolphin, Newport Pagnell — an informal, out-of-hours format designed for real conversations rather than formal pitches.
 Tickets at £9.77. Worth pencilling in as a low-friction way to keep the local network warm ahead of MK Tech Week the following week.

**Local news**

- **City of Culture bid.** 
MK is actively seeking public backing for its bid to become UK City of Culture 2029
 — the council is running a campaign for residents and businesses to register support. A successful bid would bring significant national arts investment and profile to the city.

- **Stantonbury School.** 
Stantonbury School has been placed in special measures following an Ofsted inspection
 — a significant local story given it's one of the larger secondaries. Worth monitoring if it triggers wider debate at council level about school standards and capacity in the city.

- **Coach connectivity.** 
The City Council is championing the growth of sustainable coach services for residents and visitors through FlixBus
 — a quiet but practical transport development that improves intercity connectivity without adding to road traffic.

- **Community.** 
A Stagecoach Midlands driver, Ben Corr, has been recognised after stopping his bus to talk down a man threatening to jump from a bridge
 — awarded Star of the Month, and widely noted locally.

sections.title: News
sections.body:
The search results for purely UK-domestic news this morning are thin — most indexed results on UK politics and economy are from earlier this week (6–7 August), which were already covered in yesterday's section. However, there is a clear, fresh story on Gaza from 9–10 August via Reuters/NBC/Al Jazeera that genuinely moves the situation on. Here is the section:

---

**Gaza peace process fractures.** 
Netanyahu publicly rejected Trump's 15-point Gaza peace plan at a Cabinet meeting on Sunday, saying "Israel rejects the 15-point document" and that the IDF will not withdraw until Hamas is fully disarmed.
 
Netanyahu is in campaign mode ahead of an October election, caught between far-right ministers opposed to any concessions and Trump, who wants progress on ending the conflict.
 
Hamas said it remained committed to implementing the plan and called on mediators to prevent any breaches from derailing it.
 
Trump's Gaza envoy warned that failure to implement the deal in full risks Hamas rearming and "increasing the risk of another October 7th."


- 
Since the ceasefire began last October, at least 1,258 people have been killed and over 4,100 wounded.


**UK — quiet morning.** No material developments on the stories covered yesterday (Burnham Budget timetable, bank tax speculation, defence spending, BP North Sea, or jobs data) have broken since. Watch for any Bank of England commentary — 
Bloomberg noted last week that rate-watchers are pressing for more signals from BoE Deputy Governor Lombardelli.
